Wow. What an amazing visual novel.

Orwell begins as a simple story about an investigator following up on a crime, but deviates into a darker story asking the player if what is for the greater good truly is ethical.

There are a few choices that will change the story significantly, and these choices will create different endings, allowing you to play through the story a few times as different investigators before the game truly "ends" so you can get the whole story.

The only con, a large one in my opinion, is that the game babies you and holds your hand. All answers are highlighted to you. Large red (!) signs appear when there is a pertinent piece of information in that story. NON-STORY SPOILER: [spoiler]At the later end of the game, you are limited on how much information you can process, meaning there is literally no skill or real cognitive function required to do your detective work.[/spoiler] For a game that has the feeling of a detective thriller, you are practically on rails to what is already being laid out for you.

Overall, this is a masterpiece of a novel, it emulates the fearmongering that comes from modern technologies, and has the potential to give you goosebumps from the twists and turns you, the lone investigator finds on the trail. While there are a couple choices that cement the final ending, the majority of the game is spelled out for you, but that's okay, this is an amazing story and worth the hand-holding.

Granted, games like the stanly parable have even less interactivity. But at least TSP had atmosphere, comedy, and an engaging naritive. This has none of that charm, with the player looking at documents for hours. And is not like Papers please either. Even though you also stare at documents, it had atmosphere, a goal, charisma, failure conditions, etc, etc. This game was absolute tedium, but a good strory could have saved it. But is the story any good? Well, if it where in a minor element of a large game, this would probably be suficant, maybe evan engaging. However, with this game basicly being an interactive movie, but without the terrible (but hillarous) FMV, or any real video, for that matter, it has a story that absolutly can not carry the entire production. If you looking for a good, narative heavy game, try Thimbleweed Park, Day of the Tentacle, Grimm Fandango, or The Stanley Parable. Just not this.

Orwell, in a not-so-subtle nod to George Orwell's criticism of totalitarianism (*CoughCommunismCough*) 1984. I've actually read 1984. It's not bad. It's not great, and quite frankly I think it's more of an observation than a story which in my eyes weakens it. It's also an incredibly quick read so I do recommend you check it out. On a scale of 1-10? Probably a 7. Amusing, but not the best. Slightly better than average.

Anyway, the gameplay of Orwell is unconventional and reminds me greatly of Papers, Please. Which is another game I should write a review on and I do recommend it. In it you scan documents for information and upload this information into a mega-database which contains details on everyone under investigation (at this time). Presumably, Orwell would be expanded to cover all citizens. In the name of peace, surely! Everyone can trust the government to know every detail about them to make sure that they're entirely safe! 

Light Spoiler Warning: Orwell is a narrative, a visual novel of sorts. I'm going to do my best to avoid spoilers.

Throughout the course of Orwell you follow the individuals of an organization called 'Thought' named after some German poem. Thought is an alleged terrorist organization. Your job is to follow the members of this organization to prevent terrorist activity. The first person you investigate is a woman with blue hair and problem glasses because of course she is. Which now presents us with our question. What scale of authoritarianism would be acceptable in the name of protecting people? As the game progresses, it gets to the point where almost the slightest connection to someone (perhaps eating lunch or seeing a movie together) is grounds for investigation. Authoritarianism seems to have a very tough job reigning itself in from being conventionally oppressive. 

You know, I could not help but giggle with glee as I listened to phone calls of people and other people got blamed for things that I did. It was glorious! And it kept happening! I felt no guilt at all for doing my job. Perhaps that's the point of the game. Thinking.jpg

The art style is... quirky. Not bad. Just quirky. The music is pretty okay too. My (small) gripe (I guess) is how long I had to wait for responses when it came to monitoring calls and SMS. I get that it's supposed to be realistic, that's the point. Not really a point against the game, I just felt that it was sometimes a little long. 

Overall, excellent game. Quite a nice length for the price ($10 at the time of posting). Of course, cheaper is always better. I think my first playthrough had a run of about 4 hours and there are multiple endings (all of which, I did not explore). It's a thumbs up from me.

Orwell had me on the edge of my proverbial seat more than once. I played the game from start to (one) end in one sitting. I observed myself become careless, abusing my power as the investigator. I made mistakes, and I felt shame because the game made me care about the characters. I made right choices and figured out secrets, and I felt excitement and pride because the game did not make it easy. 
Sure, some passages were a bit linear and less eventful, just like in a book or a movie. But there are many things to learn and discover, and everything is so perfectly arranged, down to the advertisements on the in-game websites you read. Everything has an explanation, there are virtually no plotholes (at least none that I noticed). Ultimately, I felt like I had real power and my decisions mattered. 
While Orwell is obviously a very story-driven game, the art was also quite appealing to me.

How should we EVALUATE Orwell?

Is it an anti-fascist salute to the famous novel, a revelation toward our digitalized lifestyle, or just simple satire to the authority?

This ultra-realism game is based on actual events that happened in the passed decade. The player acts as an investigator to wiretap multiple POIs in order to investigate and prevent bloodshed. And there is the old question of ethics. You know what this typical pop-cultured question is, and please don't spit that 3 line of words from our beloved author because this game is going to completely obliterate that old-fasioned image of mass-surveillance of yours. 

Because in this game, just like how emergency works in reality, freedom is at stake, and so does lives, integrity , security, and pretty much everything that make the nation stands together instead of falling apart are hanging in the balance. Things were not and will never be that simple. 

Also in the same game, you will make your best decisions based on what you believe in reality. You can be the detective, the judge, or the executioner, but unforturnately you shall never be the big brother, because he's not here and he never existed; because behind the monitor, every investigator and their superior is just common, living and breathing people that has little attitute toward his or her world, like those they observe. Thus mass-surveillance will never be mass-mind controll. So RIP Orwell, prism,electroscreen greatfirewall, KIMorputin.net or anything that attempts to turn security tool into A.I. bigbrother. Your service will be remembered. 

But why do instrument of oppression such as these still exists? This game will give you, your own, answer.

Orwell is a game about mass surveillance, its chances and dangers. You are an investigator on a case: you need to detect suspicous behaviours among the suspects and find connections between them.

For the gameplay, you find yourself in front of the Orwell interface. Here is where the scary magic happens, you connect suspects, work yourself through documents and plug into phone calls.

This simple mechanic does a very good job in presenting you a story that sucks you in. You have to chose on your own what to believe, who to trust - and what to do. Choices matter here, and you will know that soon!

Orwell is a great game that shows all facets of mass surveillance. I highly recommend it!

I'm stopping because of the mechanic: Conflicted Datachunks.

You're presented two conflicting stories and have to choose which is true.  It's fun when you can figure out why the stories conflict. Most of the time, though, there's not enough evidence.  And once you make a choice - there's no going back.

This is opposite of how we should handle conflictings ideas. It's important to avoid jumping to conclusions - something your counterpart Symes does consistently. It's important to be open to possibilities and revise your position if new valid evidence comes in.

We're all subject to confirmation bias - games can teach us how to recognize and manage it.  "Sherlock Holmes: Crimes and Punishments" is a better model for dealing with difficult, uncertain decisions.

I'm happy Osmotic Studios is tackling such weighty topics in their games, but it also means the skills the player practices need to build solid foundations for dealing with those issues.

Orwell is a gripping techno-thriller about the consequences of mass surveillance.

In the game, you take on the role of an "Investigator" and soon find yourself tasked with using the mass surveillance system "Orwell" to uncover the perpetrators behind a terrorist attack. However, things soon become a lot more complicated as you creep through the private lives of seemingly innocent citizens, trawling through their social media accounts, phone calls and even private files in an effort to uncover evidence.

From a gameplay perspective, Orwell is very much what I would call an "interactive story". You'll be doing a lot of reading, but the writing is excellent and the feeling of doing detective work will keep you hooked. This is very much the game equivalent of a page-turner.

I don't want to spoil the story, so suffice to say that I found it highly engaging and I was interested all the way through to the end. Not only that, but there are several places in the game where your decisions weigh unusually heavily and will affect the outcome of the story. Finally, the game gives an eerie look into a not-so distant future where we are under the watchful eye of a mass surveillance system. In this day and age of interconnectedness, the plot of Orwell is disturbingly believable.

During my time with Orwell I experienced a few technical issues, including slowdowns and glitches that required ALT+F4:ing out of the game and restarting it. These disruptions did detract a bit from the overall impression of the game, but not much.

All in all, I highly recommend Orwell. If you enjoyed "Papers, Please" I'm sure you will enjoy Orwell.

A game about surveillance, justice, the truth, and YOUR privacy.
Orwell, as you'd expect from the title, is set in a dystopian country where the people have lost their privacy, and are constantly watched by a totalitarian government. Unlike other dystopian fiction, Orwell tackles very real themes with depth, putting YOU in the shoes of the government this time. Snoop around people's personal data, invade their computers, listen to their conversations. All for the betterment of the country... Right? 
Very well worth the money. Compelling story, nice UI and soundtrack; and at the end you'll probably be much careful with what you post on Facebook.

How do I describe this game? Well, in short, AMAZING. This game gives us an inside look of what it's like to work for Big Brother. The controls are really easy to use and isn't like the average story game you can find. In this game, your research influences the fates of the suspects to the crime. Big Brother is watching. This game is basically an adaptation of George Orwell's 1984 hence the name 'Orwell'. You are an investigator who is helping your superiors by getting information about people under suspicion from internet, personal devices and private documents. But be self-aware, that once someone has crossed this line, they cease to be an innocent person. Will you be able to make the right decision when the time is right?
Great game !

I study Counter Terrorism and Intelligence and my wow they get a lot of things right. Finally a game that allows me to apply my knowledge :P But in all seriousness whilst the story is short and the mechanics are rather simple, the depth is spectacular. The real issue of "Security or Liberty" as I like to put it is perfectly encapsulated by this game. And also the ethics of invading privacy even if authorised by warrant. 

Whats also great is that the game doesnt make you feel bad for having conservative viewpoint like myself. I Honestly prefer security over some liberty but this game makes you realise how grey the whole issue is rather than black and white. Its a reality we face in modern times with technology as capable as it is.

Overall the game is fantastic, good soundtrack, interaction and the ability to change the way events unfold just gives a lot of depth. All I would say is its rather short (those 5 hours are about all I can squeeze out without starting again) and potentially not a game for everyone, especially those who dont get involved in narrative based games.

[i]Orwell[/i] is a short game with two very simple mechanics: 1) collect information (e.g. read through documents, listen in on conversations); and 2) decide which information to pass onto your employer.

There is no real challenge in the first of these tasks, since information that [b]might[/b] be relevant is automatically highlighted for you as you read.  The second task is technically simple, but morally and ethically difficult -- what you choose to share about a particular target decides their fate -- and it's here that [i]Orwell[/i] shines.

Pleasantly surprised at how immersive this game was, once you really get into it. I couldn't stop playing until I'd finished the story! It took me 5 hours although I suspect it could be completed much quicker if you don't read everything or think so long about which choices to make. I will definitely play again and try the different endings. 

Without giving too much away, you're hired to online stalk some people the state considers suspicious. You get to choose which pieces of information you pass along to them and you can be very misleading if you choose. You can get people killed, you can expose the government, you can get the right or the wrong people imprisoned and best of all, you will definitely find yourself asking some very big questions about the world we live in and an individuals right to privacy.

It's a good game, would definitely recommend it. The story is nice and has good depth to it but the endling fell a bit flat for me. But with that in mind, I did play it through several times and in my opinion it holds up. The biggest gripe I have with it is that I can't skip forward in conversations.

Orwell is a rather mechanically simple game about seemingly objective system of surveillance and crime prevention. There was a terrorist attack and you, the independent investigator with no bias, need to feed the Orwell system with bits and pieces of information you find on possible suspects and connected people. Digging through public information, going on their social networks and blogs and digging deep, wiretapping calls and reading chats. With the idea being that there a specific data pieces that can objectively help the investigation.

Of course, bits and pieces, torn out of context, are not necessarily simple to use "objectively" and everything can be spun and shaped in very biased directions. Which is shown in, surprisingly, mild and creeping way, for which I can praise the developers. While it doesn't touch upon more extreme examples of both governmental and public misuse of available data, which, I felt, should've been also covered, it gets the point across, not just about more in your face Orwellian government controlled things, but about a lot of things suffering from the same misuse and shaping of out of context materials - sensationalism in media, information wars between and within countries, internet heated discussions gone wrong and just about the faults of human arguments in general. There's a next "season" of the game announced already so there's good potential they can cover more important topics in the future, but I just hope they keep the tightly story-driven element at the core as it really is what keeps it interesting.

Absolutely amazing game. The characters are very in depth and every time you think you have things figured out and the ending predicted it throws you for a whole new loop and make you completely reconsider everything you thought you knew. Fun and original gameplay, intuitive systems and amazing moral choices and endings. Thank you for letting me experience this. 10/10.

Some games you play because you want to unwind, or you want to build things, or you just want to win against other people.

This isn't one of those games. This one forces you to think about the new age of media and how information is stored and processed.

I don't really want to talk about the things in the game, because I don't want to spoil the experience for you. This isn't really a game where you have familiar mechanics, or great graphics. It's mainly a story told to you in a way that forces you to act in how you view the concept of power. If you haven't played the game yet, don't read the next paragraph.

I feel the issue with this game is mainly how much you care about being in control and in power. If you are living in a country that is democratic on paper but just shy of being a fascist nation, you prefer to be in power. There is no safety for you unless you think and act like 'one of them'.

And that is fun. For me, the end of the game was largely focused on that. It was too fun to spy on people, too fun to find clues and watch them squirm. It was so fun, in fact, that the peoples whose lives you hurt mean nothing, and not only in a video game way. In the end, they were just images and phrases in a social media site out of thousands, and they all had the same issues and favourite colours and likes and dislikes. The breach of privacy that we feel stems only if we are not the ones making the breaches, and if you think about it, we all do it in a way. Stalking is exactly that. It is the power to follow someone on a social media without them knowing.

I wanted to gather my thoughts a little bit more to write something more focused but I'm not sure I will be able to.

TLDR: This is a game about control and power. It makes you experience it and think about it. It's short but fun in it's own way.

I have been a big fan of George Orwell from the age of seventeen and have looked forward to a game that could show how powerful his words were and be understood by many in a way books may no longer get across and I find people (especially younger people) do not quite seem to understand how powerful Big Brother is and the depth of information that can be found on them in the modern day. 

I felt this game portrayed this very well. I found no bugs with the game which was great.

I found it quite scary on how simple the game put across the invasion of a persons private life could be but at the same time I would like to think such has prevented casualties occuring.
